title: From Issue to Reviewed PR
subtitle: GitHub Copilot in VS Code · Intermediate

scenes.title: Fix a bug. Verify every step.
scenes.body: One order validator. One small change. One peer-reviewed PR.
scenes.code: is_valid_quantity(0)
scenes.result: True  ← zero should be rejected
scenes.focus: Zero returns true even though the issue says reject it
scenes.action: Compare the starting validator with the issue.
scenes.narration: Here’s a small bug that makes a useful full walkthrough. The order validator accepts zero. The issue says an order needs at least one item. We’ll trace the cause in Copilot Plan, make the change in Agent, and show both test runs. Then we’ll hand the pull request to a teammate, who reviews it with GitHub CLI.

scenes.title: Read the issue and set the target
scenes.body: The validator currently accepts an order with zero items.
scenes.code:
Issue #17: Reject zero quantities
Accept 1 and 5. Reject 0 and -1.
Preserve the public function signature.
scenes.result: A checkable rule for the fix.
scenes.focus: The issue lists accepted and rejected inputs
scenes.action: Read issue seventeen and copy its acceptance cases.
scenes.narration: Open the training issue. We want one and five to pass, and zero and negative one to fail. We also want to keep the existing function signature. Those details make the work easy to check. For your own training repository, use the actual issue number GitHub assigned. Seventeen is the number in this example.

scenes.title: Scope the change in Plan
scenes.body: Give Copilot the issue and the relevant source and test files.
scenes.code:
Attach issue #17, order_quantity.py, and the tests.
Find the cause and propose the smallest regression.
List the affected files and stop after the plan.
scenes.result:
Cause: the equality admits zero.
Missing test: an assertion for zero.
scenes.focus: The plan names one condition and one missing boundary test
scenes.action: Attach the issue and two files in Copilot Plan.
scenes.narration: In VS Code, open Copilot Chat and select Plan when it’s available. Add the issue, the validator, and the existing tests. Ask why zero gets through and which test would expose it. The plan should point to the equality in the return line and propose a new zero test. Read both files and agree on the scope before changing them.

scenes.title: Make the test fail first
scenes.body: Switch to Agent and ask it to add only the regression test.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... FAIL
AssertionError: True is not false
scenes.focus: The new assertion fails because zero still returns true
scenes.action: In Agent, request only the new test and run it remotely.
scenes.narration: Switch to Agent and ask for the test first. Inspect the edit and confirm the source comparison has stayed the same. Run the approved test command on a checkout with that edit. Find the line for the zero test. We expected this failure because the old implementation still returns true. If you see an import error instead, sort out the test setup first.

scenes.title: Fix the condition and run it again
scenes.body: The comparison changes. The interface stays the same.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... ok
Ran 4 tests. OK
scenes.focus: Four tests pass after equality is removed
scenes.action: Apply the agreed comparison change and rerun the same suite.
scenes.narration: Now make the one-line fix. When we remove equality, zero no longer satisfies the condition. One and five still do, and negative one still fails it. Run the same suite in the approved environment. The result should say four tests ran and passed. Keep the red and green results together so your teammate can see what the new test proved.

scenes.title: Review the diff before publishing
scenes.body: Match both files to the issue and the test evidence.
scenes.code:
-    return quantity >= 0
+    return quantity > 0
+    self.assertFalse(is_valid_quantity(0))
scenes.result: Published branch: fix/reject-zero-quantity
scenes.focus: The diff contains the validator change and its new test
scenes.action: Open Source Control, inspect the two diffs and publish the branch.
scenes.narration: Open Source Control in VS Code. Check the validator diff for the comparison change, then open the test diff and find the zero assertion. Check that no unrelated file came along. Commit these two changes on the training feature branch and publish the branch through Source Control. You now have a small patch, with each change tied to the issue.

scenes.title: Open the PR with evidence
scenes.body: Use the approved remote terminal once the branch is published.
scenes.code:
gh pr create --base main \
  --title "Reject zero order quantities" \
  --body-file pr-body.md
scenes.result:
PR #42 created.
Body links #17 and records red/green evidence.
scenes.focus: The PR body links the issue and records the test results
scenes.action: Create the PR from the published branch in the approved terminal.
scenes.narration: In the approved remote terminal, use an authorized author account and a checkout of the published branch. Prepare a short pull request body. Include the change, the red and green test evidence, and the issue link. Open the pull request with GitHub CLI. Our example receives number forty-two. Give that number to a separate authorized teammate.

scenes.title: Review the PR from the terminal
scenes.body: A teammate uses their own authorized account and reviews the evidence.
scenes.code:
gh pr view 42
gh pr diff 42
gh pr checks 42
gh pr review 42 --approve
scenes.result: The authorized peer records their decision.
scenes.focus: The peer checks intent, diff and CI before choosing a review
scenes.action: Inspect the PR with GitHub CLI under the reviewer’s account.
scenes.narration: The reviewer uses their own account in the approved terminal. Read the pull request, inspect the diff, and check the required results for that revision. If the evidence supports approval, the human reviewer records it. If something is missing, they request a specific change. This is the teammate’s decision. We’ll practice both outcomes in the dedicated review lesson.

scenes.title: Run the same workflow yourself
scenes.body: Try it on another issue in the training repository.
scenes.code: Issue → Plan → Agent → Verified diff → PR → Peer review
scenes.result: A teammate can replay the evidence.
scenes.focus: The final handover contains the issue, test proof and a peer decision
scenes.action: Repeat the workflow on a second synthetic issue.
scenes.narration: Look back at what you can hand over. There’s an issue with clear inputs, a small diff, a test that failed then passed, and a peer decision. Try the same workflow on another synthetic issue. Replace the example identifiers with your own training issue and pull request. Ask your teammate to tell you which evidence they used.

title: Debug with a Failing Test
subtitle: GitHub Copilot in VS Code · Intermediate

sources.label: Test-driven development with AI in VS Code

scenes.title: State the symptom precisely
scenes.body: Reduce the issue to one input and two observable answers.
scenes.narration: The report says zero orders slip through. Let’s translate that into a call we can test. When the validator receives zero, it currently returns true. The issue requires false. The inputs one and five should still pass, and negative one should still fail. Keep that expected behavior in view while we investigate what the code actually does.
scenes.code:
is_valid_quantity(0)
Expected: False
Observed: True
scenes.result: Boundary case identified: zero units.
scenes.focus: The observed value and required value disagree at zero
scenes.action: Read the training issue and write down the exact failing example.

scenes.title: Check the starting suite
scenes.body: Run the existing tests on the starting revision.
scenes.narration: Run the existing tests from the training checkout in the approved environment. The suite goes green. Now read the test names. There’s one test each for one, five, and negative one. There’s no zero case. That's why a green result can coexist with the bug. Record the checkout and the exact test command so we can repeat the check consistently.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_accepts_one ... ok
test_accepts_five ... ok
test_rejects_negative_one ... ok
Ran 3 tests. OK
scenes.focus: Three tests pass and none calls the validator with zero
scenes.action: Run the baseline tests in the approved runner.

scenes.title: Turn a guess into a hypothesis
scenes.body: Ask for a prediction tied to a specific line.
scenes.narration: Open the issue, the validator, and the tests in VS Code. In Copilot Plan, ask which expression could explain this behavior. The proposed cause is the greater-than-or-equal comparison. Read the line and substitute zero. Zero equals zero, so the expression is true. Now we have a prediction. An assertion expecting false for zero should fail on the original revision.
scenes.code: return quantity >= 0
scenes.result:
Hypothesis: the equality admits zero.
Prediction: an assertFalse for zero will fail.
scenes.focus: The comparison makes a testable prediction for zero
scenes.action: Ask Plan to predict the result from the return line.

scenes.title: Add one test before fixing the code
scenes.body: Inspect the test diff and preserve the original validator.
scenes.narration: Ask Agent to add just the zero regression to the existing test class. Inspect the proposed patch. It should call the public function with zero and expect false. The validator itself should still have its original comparison. This separation is useful because the next run will tell us whether the new test can detect the reported behavior before any fix is applied.
scenes.code:
def test_rejects_zero(self):
    self.assertFalse(is_valid_quantity(0))
scenes.result: Changed file: tests/test_order_quantity.py
scenes.focus: The test-only diff adds one assertion against the public function
scenes.action: Request the regression test and inspect the test-only patch.

scenes.title: Read why the test failed
scenes.body: Confirm that the expected assertion failed for zero.
scenes.narration: Run the same suite with the new test present. Look for the zero test name and the assertion message. True was returned where false was expected. That failure supports the hypothesis. If the suite stops because of a missing import, it hasn't shown that the boundary is wrong. Fix the setup first and rerun until you have the failure you intended to test.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... FAIL
AssertionError: True is not false
Ran 4 tests. FAILED (failures=1)
scenes.focus: The expected assertion fails for the expected reason
scenes.action: Run the updated suite and find the zero assertion failure.

scenes.title: Change the comparison and rerun
scenes.body: The regression and the existing cases should all pass.
scenes.narration: Change greater than or equal to zero to greater than zero. Keep the assertion and the function signature as they are. Rerun the same test command on the updated checkout. Now all four cases should pass. Check the source diff and the test diff together. Each one should answer a part of the issue you started with.
scenes.code:
-    return quantity >= 0
+    return quantity > 0
scenes.result:
test_rejects_zero ... ok
Ran 4 tests. OK
scenes.focus: The same four-case suite passes after the one-line fix
scenes.action: Apply the one-line fix and rerun the same command.

scenes.title: Leave evidence a teammate can replay
scenes.body: Explain the cause and point to both test runs.
scenes.narration: Let’s turn the investigation into something another engineer can replay. Record the zero input, the original comparison, and both test results. Say which revision produced each output. Then explain why one still passes and negative one still fails. If you can answer from the source and the tests, you've verified the change as well as the proposed diagnosis.
scenes.code:
Input: 0
Cause: equality in the boundary check
Before: one assertion fails
After: four tests pass
scenes.result: A testable explanation of the change.
scenes.focus: A teammate can replay the failure and the passing run
scenes.action: Write a short reproduction note from the two outputs.

title: Review a Pull Request with GitHub CLI
subtitle: Human peer review · Intermediate

scenes.title: Start in the reviewer’s account
scenes.body: Confirm the account and the training repository before review.
scenes.narration: This time you’re the reviewer. In the approved remote terminal, confirm that GitHub CLI is using your own authorized account and that you are in the training repository. The author sends you pull request forty-two. Open that request for this exercise. We’ll check the intent first, then the actual patch, and finally the checks for the revision you’re reviewing.
scenes.code:
gh auth status
gh repo view --json nameWithOwner
scenes.result: Training context confirmed: orders-lab.
scenes.focus: The reviewer account and training repository are visible
scenes.action: Confirm GitHub CLI’s active account and repository.

scenes.title: Read the intent and the scope
scenes.body: Find the linked issue, the change summary and test evidence.
scenes.narration: Run the GitHub CLI view command for pull request forty-two. Read the title and the issue link. The author says zero should be rejected and all four unit tests now pass. That tells you what to look for. Keep the issue open beside the terminal so you can compare the requested behavior with the change you’re about to inspect.
scenes.code: gh pr view 42
scenes.result:
Reject zero order quantities
Closes #17
Validation: four unit tests passed.
scenes.focus: The PR describes the issue and the author’s claimed evidence
scenes.action: Read the PR title, body and linked issue.

scenes.title: Read the changed lines yourself
scenes.body: Match the implementation and test to the stated behavior.
scenes.narration: Now view the actual diff. The main change removes equality at the boundary. The second change adds a test that calls the validator with zero. Ask yourself whether that test would fail on the old code. This is the difference between seeing a test name and seeing a test that proves the relevant behavior.
scenes.code: gh pr diff 42
scenes.result:
-    return quantity >= 0
+    return quantity > 0
+    self.assertFalse(is_valid_quantity(0))
scenes.focus: The diff shows both the changed condition and a test for zero
scenes.action: Read the patch and locate the assertion that detects the bug.

scenes.title: Confirm the configured checks
scenes.body: Review the state of the checks for the current revision.
scenes.narration: Look up the pull request’s required checks. In the training example, the unit test check is required. Open its run if you need to confirm which suite it executed. If the checks are pending, wait for the result. If the author pushes again, refresh the diff and checks for the new head before making your decision.
scenes.code:
gh pr checks 42 --required
gh pr view 42 --json headRefOid
scenes.result:
Unit tests    pass
Head revision recorded for this review.
scenes.focus: The expected CI check applies to the reviewed head revision
scenes.action: Check required statuses and note the current head revision.

scenes.title: Request a specific correction
scenes.body: Use this branch of the exercise if the evidence is incomplete.
scenes.narration: Here’s the alternate outcome. The checks are green, but the test added in this version exercises one and never calls the validator with zero. That leaves the bug untested. Use the request-changes option and ask for the missing assertion. Give the author a specific behavior to verify. Review the new revision after they address it.
scenes.code:
gh pr review 42 --request-changes \
  --body 'Add a test that calls the validator with zero.'
scenes.result: Record a request with an actionable reason.
scenes.focus: An actionable review asks for the missing zero assertion
scenes.action: In the alternate scenario, record a targeted change request.

scenes.title: Approve when the evidence supports it
scenes.body: The authorized peer submits the review under their own identity.
scenes.narration: Return to the version with the right condition and the actual zero test. If you’ve checked the diff and the required results, you can approve with a short statement of what you verified. Submit the review from your account, then read back the reviews on the pull request. Confirm your decision was saved to the intended request.
scenes.code:
gh pr review 42 --approve \
  --body 'Verified the zero regression and required checks.'
gh pr view 42 --json reviews
scenes.result: Review recorded for the peer account.
scenes.focus: The saved review belongs to the authorized peer
scenes.action: For sufficient evidence, submit and confirm your human approval.

scenes.title: Explain the evidence behind your decision
scenes.body: Give a teammate enough detail to verify the review.
scenes.narration: Pair up and swap author and reviewer roles. Give each reviewer an issue, a pull request, and the check results. In one run, the evidence is complete. In the other, leave out the test for the key input. Ask the reviewer to explain their decision in one sentence. It should tell the author what was verified or what needs to change.
scenes.code: Intent → Diff → Required checks → Decision
scenes.result: A human review with a verifiable reason.
scenes.focus: The review reason names the requirement, patch and check
scenes.action: Switch roles with a teammate and practice both decisions.

title: Reusable Prompts and Repository Instructions
subtitle: GitHub Copilot in VS Code · Intermediate

scenes.title: Identify what changes from one task to the next
scenes.body: Keep task inputs and durable project conventions easy to find.
scenes.narration: Picture two issues in the same repository. One is about zero quantities. Another asks for a clearer error message. The issue ID and expected behavior change. The location of the test suite may stay the same across both. Put recurring project conventions where the agent can load them, and keep the individual issue details in the prompt you send for that task.
scenes.code:
Current task: issue #17 and expected behavior
Repository: tests live in tests/
Repository: use the existing unittest suite
scenes.result: Task inputs and durable conventions identified.
scenes.focus: The issue changes but the test convention carries across tasks
scenes.action: Sort the task details and enduring project conventions.

scenes.title: Capture a prompt your team can reuse
scenes.body: Keep a named template and fill in its variable inputs.
scenes.narration: Open a Markdown template in the training repository. Write a request that takes an issue and the current source and tests as inputs. Ask for the proposed edit, the affected files, and a way to verify it. The template should end at a plan you can review. On the approved Copilot setup, paste the filled-in text into chat to run it.
scenes.code:
Read issue [id] and the attached source and tests.
Propose the smallest edit and a regression test.
List the files, validation steps and open questions.
Stop after the plan for human review.
scenes.result: Template: docs/prompts/plan-a-fix.md
scenes.focus: The reusable template exposes its variable inputs
scenes.action: Save a plain Markdown planning prompt with placeholders.

scenes.title: Supply current evidence at invocation
scenes.body: Use the template with source files and tests from the same revision.
scenes.narration: Start Plan in the current branch and attach the issue, validator, and matching test file. Paste the template with the issue reference filled in. The response should identify the existing comparison and explain why a zero test would expose it. Open the cited lines and check them yourself. If a file name is unfamiliar, confirm it in the workspace before accepting the plan.
scenes.code:
Issue #17
order_quantity.py
tests/test_order_quantity.py
scenes.result: Plan names the condition and the missing zero test.
scenes.focus: The plan traces observations to the three current attachments
scenes.action: Fill the prompt and attach the original issue, function and tests.

scenes.title: Record a project convention once
scenes.body: Keep the instructions concrete and versioned with the code.
scenes.narration: Open the repository root in VS Code. For this Copilot example, find or create the project instructions file in the dot GitHub folder. Add the convention that unit tests use the existing unittest suite under tests. Keep the rule short and include a reliable reference for the verification command. If instructions already exist, edit the existing guidance with your team.
scenes.code:
# Order validator conventions
- Use unittest for unit tests under tests/.
- Preserve public signatures unless the issue says otherwise.
- See README.md for the approved verification command.
scenes.result: Saved: .github/copilot-instructions.md
scenes.focus: The repository instructions name test location and framework
scenes.action: Add one concrete convention to the supported instruction file.

scenes.title: Check that Copilot loaded the instructions
scenes.body: Verify discovery and actual behavior in a new chat.
scenes.narration: Open the agent customizations view and find the instruction file. Then start a fresh chat in the same workspace. Ask for a regression plan without repeating the test convention. Where your client shows references, confirm the file was included. Read the proposed test location and framework. File discovery and correct use give you two different things to check.
scenes.code: Plan one regression test for the zero-quantity issue.
scenes.result: File discovered. Plan uses the existing unittest suite.
scenes.focus: A fresh session discovers the file and proposes the expected test
scenes.action: Verify the instruction is loaded and test a fresh plan.

scenes.title: Give each type of guidance a clear role
scenes.body: Use a task template, project instructions and real review controls.
scenes.narration: The prompt asks for a particular piece of work. The instruction file supplies reusable project conventions. Required checks and actual tool permissions enforce separate boundaries. Some VS Code versions also offer runnable prompt files, with support depending on the selected harness. The Markdown template in this example is ready to paste. In the next lesson, we’ll make a recurring procedure into a skill.
scenes.code:
Prompt template → task request
Instruction file → project conventions
Permissions and checks → enforcement
scenes.result: Review each file where its behavior is observable.
scenes.focus: Task prompts, conventions and permission controls have distinct jobs
scenes.action: Connect each piece of guidance to what it affects.

scenes.title: Try a second issue and compare the plan
scenes.body: Change the issue and check which guidance still applies.
scenes.narration: Use the template for a second synthetic issue. Swap the issue reference and attach the current files for that task. Compare the two plans and find one part that changed because the requirement changed. Then find the test convention that carried over. A teammate should be able to reproduce that setup in a fresh session with the same project files.
scenes.code:
New issue → new attachments → new plan
Same repository → same test conventions
scenes.result: A teammate can reproduce the setup in a fresh chat.
scenes.focus: A new issue changes the plan while the test convention remains
scenes.action: Run the same template with a second issue and fresh attachments.

title: What Is a Skill? Build Your First One
subtitle: Agent Skills in VS Code · Intermediate

sources.label: Create Agent Skills in VS Code

scenes.title: Find a task the team repeats
scenes.body: Package a pull request evidence checklist for reuse.
scenes.narration: Think about what you do before handing off a pull request. You check the issue, summarize the diff, and share the result of the tests. If you ask for that same draft often, you can give the assistant a skill with this procedure. We’ll use a synthetic example and make the output a draft that the human author can review.
scenes.code:
Input: issue, diff and test output
Procedure: check and summarize the evidence
Output: a draft for the human author
scenes.result: Chosen skill: prepare pull request evidence.
scenes.focus: An issue, diff and test output produce one reusable draft
scenes.action: Choose the recurring PR evidence task for the first skill.

scenes.title: Name the skill and say when it applies
scenes.body: Use the skill folder supported by the Copilot setup.
scenes.narration: In the training repository, open the supported project skills location for Copilot. This example puts a folder named prepare P R evidence under dot GitHub skills. Add a file named skill dot M D. Give it a matching name and a short description that says which task it helps with. Both of those fields are useful when you verify discovery.
scenes.code:
---
name: prepare-pr-evidence
description: Draft evidence for a training pull request.
---
scenes.result: .github/skills/prepare-pr-evidence/SKILL.md
scenes.focus: The folder name and skill name match
scenes.action: Create and name SKILL.md in the approved project skill folder.

scenes.title: Define the steps and intended output
scenes.body: Make missing evidence visible in the draft.
scenes.narration: In the body, tell the skill to read the supplied issue and diff, check the test output, and return a draft with change and verification evidence. Include a step for missing items. If no test output is supplied, the draft should say verification is missing. Keep this first skill focused on preparing text for a human to review.
scenes.code:
1. Read the provided issue and diff.
2. Check the supplied test output.
3. Draft: Issue, Change, Verification, Gaps.
If data is missing, identify the gap.
Return text for the human author to review.
scenes.result: The scope ends with a draft.
scenes.focus: The skill describes inputs, steps and what to do when proof is missing
scenes.action: Write the small procedure and its expected draft sections.

scenes.eyebrow: COPILOT · INVOKE IN A FRESH CHAT
scenes.title: Discover and try the skill
scenes.body: Invoke it with the synthetic order validator change.
scenes.narration: Open a fresh Copilot chat and confirm the skill is listed in the customizations view. If your setup supports it, choose the skill from the slash menu. Attach the synthetic issue, patch, and passing test output. Now compare each draft claim with its source. In this example, the issue is seventeen, zero is rejected, and the supplied run shows four passing tests.
scenes.code:
/prepare-pr-evidence
Attach issue #17, the diff and the test output.
scenes.result:
Issue #17
Change: zero is rejected.
Verification: four unit tests passed.
Gaps: none in the supplied training evidence.
scenes.focus: The draft’s claims match the supplied issue, diff and test output
scenes.action: Invoke the skill in Copilot using the synthetic inputs.

scenes.title: Check what happens when proof is missing
scenes.body: Run the same skill with the test output omitted.
scenes.narration: Try again with the test output missing. Read what the skill says about verification. The expected result is a visible gap that the author can fill. If it claims the tests passed based only on the PR description, revise the body and rerun. Then try an unrelated request and see whether the description makes the skill’s intended scope clear.
scenes.code:
Inputs: issue and diff only
Expected: mark verification as missing
scenes.result: Verification gap surfaced for the human author.
scenes.focus: Missing test proof is flagged instead of reported as a pass
scenes.action: Retry in a fresh chat without test output.

scenes.title: Separate procedures from access
scenes.body: A procedure can refer to tools inside the approved boundary.
scenes.narration: Compare this skill with the repository instruction file. The instruction file describes conventions for work in this project. The skill carries a repeatable procedure you can invoke. Tools let the agent perform actions such as reading a supplied file. An approved M C P server can expose more tools or resources. Our example works with supplied training evidence, and the environment still controls access.
scenes.code:
Instructions → project conventions
Skill → reusable procedure
Tool → callable action
MCP → connection to a server
scenes.result: Review the skill and its dependencies before sharing.
scenes.focus: A skill provides steps while a tool provides a callable action
scenes.action: Identify one instruction, skill, tool and connector example.

scenes.title: Write a second skill with two test cases
scenes.body: Choose a recurring task and define its limits.
scenes.narration: Pick another repeated task, like summarizing a failed test for an author. Write a small skill with a clear trigger, steps, and expected output. Try it with complete input and again with one item missing. Ask a teammate to judge each result from the evidence. If they can explain when the skill applies and spot missing proof, you have a useful procedure to share.
scenes.code:
Candidate: summarize a failing test
Case A: failure output supplied
Case B: failure output missing
scenes.result: An invocable procedure with two observable tests.
scenes.focus: Two test cases demonstrate when the skill is useful
scenes.action: Draft a second skill and test complete and incomplete evidence.

title: Build a Workflow with Review Checkpoints
subtitle: Copilot, CI and human review · Intermediate

scenes.title: Map the work before delegating a step
scenes.body: Give every checkpoint an owner and evidence.
scenes.narration: Let’s put the earlier lessons together. A workflow tells us what happens next and when we should stop. Begin with the issue and plan, then prove the bug with a failing test. Apply the fix, run the suite, and hand off the pull request. At each point, name the person who checks the evidence before the next step goes ahead.
scenes.code:
Issue → Plan → Human scope review
Failing test → Fix → Passing tests
Author diff review → PR → Peer review
scenes.result: Each handoff has evidence and an owner.
scenes.focus: Every handoff names a decision owner and evidence
scenes.action: Draw the workflow from issue through independent review.

scenes.title: Review the plan before editing
scenes.body: The author checks the intended behavior and allowed change.
scenes.narration: Start in Plan and supply the issue, source, and tests. The proposal should add one assertion and change one comparison while keeping the public signature. The author reads the plan against the issue. If a new dependency or signature change appears, send the plan back for revision. Begin editing once the proposed scope fits the requirement.
scenes.code:
Keep is_valid_quantity(quantity: int) -> bool.
Add an assertion for quantity zero.
Change only the boundary comparison.
scenes.result: Author accepts scope after checking the issue.
scenes.focus: The author approves a specific scope with an unchanged signature
scenes.action: Compare the Plan output with the issue before allowing edits.

scenes.title: Verify that the test detects the defect
scenes.body: Let the expected failure authorize the next coding step.
scenes.narration: Add the regression test and run it in the approved environment. The useful failure names zero and shows that the validator returned true. If the test command never ran, or an import failed, return to the setup and repeat it. The author should be able to point to evidence that this assertion detects this defect on the original revision.
scenes.code: python -B -m unittest discover -s tests -v
scenes.result:
Expected before the fix
test_rejects_zero ... FAIL
AssertionError: True is not false
scenes.focus: The red check proves the specific regression before the fix
scenes.action: Run the test-only revision and confirm the expected assertion failure.

scenes.title: Stop when validation remains red
scenes.body: Review the approved change and require the expected passing run.
scenes.narration: After the fix, rerun the same tests. If the zero case still fails or an existing case breaks, pause and inspect the change. If all four pass, check the remaining diff and save the run output. This checkpoint uses the result of the actual suite. A plausible summary from the agent can explain the change while the test output provides the evidence.
scenes.code:
Pass → attach the test output
Fail → inspect, adjust and rerun
scenes.result: All four tests pass in the completed example.
scenes.focus: A failing verification returns the work to the author
scenes.action: Rerun the suite and choose whether the workflow can continue.

scenes.title: Prepare evidence for the pull request
scenes.body: Tie the issue, patch and checks to the same change.
scenes.narration: Use the skill from the previous lesson to organize the handover. Give it the issue, the patch, and the test output you verified. Read its draft and correct any unsupported claim. The author then opens the pull request through the approved workflow. In the training repository, the configured CI checks provide additional evidence about the revision the peer will see.
scenes.code:
Closes #17
Changed: reject zero at the validator boundary
Regression: test_rejects_zero
Verification: four unit tests passed
scenes.result: PR #42 is ready for separate peer review.
scenes.focus: The PR ties the issue, exact diff and run output together
scenes.action: Run the evidence skill and check the resulting draft.

scenes.title: Let the peer make the review decision
scenes.body: A teammate reviews the revision and required checks with GitHub CLI.
scenes.narration: Now hand the pull request number to a teammate. They use their authorized terminal account to read the PR, inspect the patch, and check the required results. They decide whether to approve or ask for a correction. Their review and the configured merge rules are part of the workflow. The author's agent can assist with the draft, while the peer records their own decision.
scenes.code:
gh pr view 42
gh pr diff 42
gh pr checks 42 --required
scenes.result: Peer decision: approve or request a specific change.
scenes.focus: The human reviewer decides after checking the current PR and CI
scenes.action: Let the peer inspect the PR and submit their own decision.

scenes.title: Dry-run both outcomes
scenes.body: Demonstrate a successful handoff and one blocked branch.
scenes.narration: Try the workflow twice with a teammate. Once, run it with the complete evidence and record the review outcome. Again, remove the regression output or simulate a failing required check. Say where work stops and what would let it resume. The rehearsal is successful when both of you can name the owner, evidence, and next action for either outcome.
scenes.code:
A: Scope accepted, tests pass, peer reviews
B: Verification missing, work returns to author
scenes.result: A documented workflow with a tested stop condition.
scenes.focus: The rehearsal demonstrates both success and a justified stop
scenes.action: Dry-run a passing case and a case with missing evidence.
